newsitem.title: USA: LA authority releases study on yield-burn charges.
newsitem.headline: LA authority releases study on yield-burn charges.

text.p: Wall Street's top two managers of bond refundings allegedly reaped at least $186 million in "yield burning" profits between 1990 and 1995, economists hired by the Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportion Authority charged in a letter issued on Tuesday.

These and other findings by the Michel/Shaked Group, a Boston consulting firm, were outlined in a 43-page comment letter that authority lawyers Phillips & Cohen sent to the Internal Revenue Service on Tuesday.

The authority said the $1.3 trillion municipal bond market has been rocked by allegations that bond underwriters overcharge issuers for U.S. Treasuries bought in the open market and used in bond financing transactions.

The practice is known as "yield burning" because a bond firm charging higher prices than it paid for the Treasuries can avoid breaking federal restrictions on "arbitrage" profits while still forcing the municipality or other issuer to accept a lower yield on Treasuries.

The IRS in July announced a process by which localities that paid more than fair market value for the Treasury securities they placed into bond escrows can avoid having interest on their bonds declared taxable by IRS.
But the LA authority said Wall Street firms should be stuck with the bill since they "expoited and deceived" municipalities and "profited handsomely."

The Michel/Shaked group priced 104 adavance refunding escrow deals and concluded that on average, noncompetitive deals had "unjustified markups" of about $4 per $1,000 per bond," the authority's comment letter says.

"The top two senior managers and Lazard Freres (& Co.) were financial advisers and senior managers for $30.202 billion, $27.853 billion and $14.147 billion of negotiated advance refunding transactions," the consultants said.

"Even if only 80 percent of these deals were affected by the average $4 a bond markup, they would have made approximately, $97 million, $89 million and $45 million, respectively in yield burning profits," the report said.
Last April, the Los Angeles County transit authority filed a $14 million lawsuit against Lazard Freres & Co. in the first court test of yield burning charges.
The economists said no U.S. state or territory is spared from yield burning damages, and lists what it calculates as each entity's bill.
California, New York, Texas and Florida face top costs, at $88.8 million, $82.1 million, $70.3 million and $58.5 million respectively, the study says.
South Dakota, the Virgin Islands, North Dakota, Montana and Wyoming have the smallest bills, the study says.
The report does not name the two industry leaders for senior managing negotiated advance refundings from 1990 to 1995.
